Description: explicit — omitted glyphs field, text renders in wrong font
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer  
It’s **not a bug**.  
When a style **doesn’t have a `glyphs` URL**, MapLibre GL JS falls back to its **local-font mode** (added in GL JS 5.11). Every `text-font` entry is treated exactly like a CSS `font-family` list:

1. The browser tries to find a **system font** with that name.  
2. If you have supplied a **web-font** (`@font-face` or `map.setFontFaces()`), the browser loads that file and uses it.  
3. If the name can’t be resolved, the browser picks its own generic fallback (usually “sans-serif”), which is why you see a “generic” font on the map.

So the map is working as designed; the only thing missing is a **real font that the browser can actually use** for the name you put in `text-font`.

---

## What’s really happening under the hood

| Step | What MapLibre does | What the browser does |
|------|-------------------|-----------------------|
| **Style parsing** | Sees no `glyphs` field → enables *local-font mode*. | – |
| **Layer rendering** | For each symbol layer it reads `text-font: ["My Fancy Font", "sans-serif"]`. | Treats that array as a CSS `font-family` list. |
| **Font resolution** | No glyph PBFs are requested (no network traffic for `/…/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`). | Looks for a **system font** named *My Fancy Font*. If none, checks the **CSS `@font-face` rules** that have been added to the page (or via `map.setFontFaces()`). |
| **If a matching font is found** | Uses the **browser’s text engine** (TinySDF for ideographs, HarfBuzz-shaped for complex scripts) to rasterise the glyphs at the required size. | The text appears in the exact font you supplied. |
| **If no matching font is found** | Falls back to the browser’s generic family (usually `sans-serif`). | You see the “generic” font. No error is thrown; the map continues to render. |

Because the fallback is **graceful**, the map never goes blank or throws a fatal error – you just get the wrong visual appearance.

---

## How to get the exact font you want

### 1. Make sure the font name matches exactly

* `text-font` values are **case-sensitive** and must match the **`font-family` name** declared in the font file (or in your `@font-face` rule).  
* Example: If the TTF’s internal name is *“My Fancy Font Regular”*, you must use that exact string (or a name you assign via `@font-face`).

```json
{
  "type": "symbol",
  "layout": {
    "text-field": ["get", "name"],
    "text-font": ["My Fancy Font Regular", "sans-serif"]
  }
}
```

### 2. Load the font into the browser

#### a. Using a classic CSS `@font-face`

```css
@font-face {
  font-family: "My Fancy Font Regular";
  src: url("https://example.com/fonts/MyFancyFont-Regular.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: normal;
  font-style: normal;
}
```

*Make sure the URL is reachable from the page (CORS headers if it’s on another origin).*

#### b. Using the MapLibre API (`map.setFontFaces`)

If you prefer to keep everything in JavaScript (e.g., you’re building a single-page app that loads fonts dynamically), you can supply the same information via the MapLibre API:

```js
map.setFontFaces({
  "My Fancy Font Regular": [
    {
      url: "https://example.com/fonts/MyFancyFont-Regular.ttf",
      // optional: limit to the Unicode range you actually need
      // unicodeRange: ["U+0000-00FF"]
    }
  ]
});
```

* `setFontFaces` can be called **any time before the first render** (or after, but you’ll need to trigger a style refresh).  
* The URLs must be fetchable by the **browser**, not by native code. If you’re also using MapLibre Native, you’ll need a separate `font-faces` entry that points at a device-accessible path.

### 3. Verify the font is actually loaded

* Open the browser’s **Network** tab and look for the font request (e.g., `MyFancyFont-Regular.woff2`).  
* In the **Console**, you can check `document.fonts.check("12px \"My Fancy Font Regular\"")` – it returns `true` when the font is ready.  
* If the check returns `false`, the font either failed to load (404/CORS) or the name doesn’t match.

### 4. Optional: Use `font-faces` in the style JSON

If you want the font information to travel with the style (useful for sharing the style file or for MapLibre Native), add a `font-faces` block at the root of the style:

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "https://example.com/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",   // optional, can be omitted
  "font-faces": {
    "My Fancy Font Regular": [
      {
        "url": "https://example.com/fonts/MyFancyFont-Regular.ttf",
        "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF"]
      }
    ]
  },
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "places",
      "type": "symbol",
      "layout": {
        "text-field": ["get", "name"],
        "text-font": ["My Fancy Font Regular", "sans-serif"]
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

*GL JS reads `font-faces` automatically (since 6.7.0) and will load the font for you, just like an `@font-face` rule.*

---

## Common pitfalls & how to fix them

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| Text appears in the browser’s default sans-serif, even though you added `@font-face`. | Font-family name mismatch (e.g., you wrote `"My Fancy Font"` but the font file’s internal name is `"My Fancy Font Regular"`). | Use the exact name you declare in `@font-face` (or rename the font in the CSS). |
| No network request for the font file at all. | You added `font-faces` in the style but are using a GL JS version **< 6.7.0** (which didn’t read `font-faces`). | Upgrade to GL JS ≥ 6.7.0 **or** add a classic `@font-face` rule in your page CSS. |
| Font request returns 404 or CORS error. | URL is wrong or the server doesn’t send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. | Correct the URL and/or configure the server to allow cross-origin requests. |
| Text looks correct on desktop but not on mobile. | Mobile browsers may not support the font format you served (e.g., only `.woff2`). | Serve a format that all target browsers understand (`.ttf`, `.woff`, `.woff2`). |
| You see a generic font **only for CJK characters**. | CJK is rendered by the `localIdeographFontFamily` path, which ignores `text-font`. | Either accept the default (fast, low-traffic) or set `localIdeographFontFamily` to a specific on-device CJK font you like. |
| Arabic/Hebrew text is garbled or displayed left-to-right. | Using a GL JS version **< 6.9.0** without loading the RTL plugin. | Upgrade to ≥ 6.9.0 (no plugin needed) **or** load the RTL plugin as shown in the skill. |

---

## TL;DR checklist

1. **Confirm you’re on GL JS ≥ 5.11** (local-font mode) – most recent releases are.  
2. **Make sure the font name in `text-font` exactly matches a font you load** (via CSS `@font-face`, `map.setFontFaces()`, or the style’s `font-faces`).  
3. **Load the font file** (WOFF2/TTF) from a URL the browser can fetch (CORS-friendly).  
4. **Verify the font loads** (`document.fonts.check(...)` or Network tab).  
5. **Refresh the map** (or call `map.triggerRepaint()` after the font is ready).  

Once those steps are satisfied, the labels will render in the exact font you specified. If you skip any of them, MapLibre gracefully falls back to the browser’s generic font – which is exactly the behavior you’re seeing now. It’s expected, not a bug.

Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step-by-step recipe** for an Android-only MapLibre Native app that: * works completely offline (no network, no external glyph server) * draws every label from fonts that live on the device (assets or the app’s private storage) * supports Latin, CJK, Arabic/Hebrew, Devanagari-type scripts, and right-to-left layout. The recipe follows the **MapLibre style spec** and the **`font-faces`** feature that was added to Native in **v11.13.0** (Android) / **v6.18.0** (iOS). If you are on an older Native version you must first upgrade – the older binaries simply cannot read `font-faces`. --- ## 1. Overview of the pieces you need | Piece | What it does | Where it lives | |------|---------------|----------------| | **`glyphs` field** | Required by the spec, but we can point it at a *dummy* URL that never returns data. Native will still try to fetch glyph PBFs, fail, and then fall back to the `font-faces` mapping. | In the style JSON (any reachable URL, e.g. `file:///android_asset/empty-glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`). | | **`font-faces` property** | Maps each `text-font` name used in the style to one or more local font files (TTF/OTF). Native loads those files via the Android asset manager or a `file://` URL, then uses HarfBuzz for shaping. | Inside the same style JSON (root level). | | **Font files** | Real TTF/OTF files that you ship with the APK (or download once and store in app-private storage). | `src/main/assets/fonts/…` (or any folder you later copy to internal storage). | | **`text-font` arrays** | The cascade of font families you want the label to try. Must match the keys you put in `font-faces`. | In each `symbol` layer that draws text. | | **Optional `localIdeographFontFamily`-like handling** | For CJK you can either let Native draw the glyphs locally (the default) or force it to use a bundled CJK font. | Set `localIdeographFontFamily` in the map options (Android SDK only) – see § 4.2. | --- ## 2. Prepare the font files 1. **Pick the fonts you need** – the easiest universal choice is the Google **Noto** family: * `NotoSans-Regular.ttf` – Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, etc. * `NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf` – Arabic script. * `NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf` – Devanagari, Hindi, etc. * `NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf` – Simplified Chinese (you can also add `CJKtc`, `CJKjp`, `CJKkr` if you need them). 2. **Copy them into the Android assets folder**: ``` app/ └─ src/ └─ main/ └─ assets/ └─ fonts/ ├─ NotoSans-Regular.ttf ├─ NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf ├─ NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf └─ NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf ``` *If you prefer to download the fonts at first-run, store them in `context.getFilesDir()/fonts/` and reference them with a `file://` URL – the same `font-faces` syntax works.* 3. **(Optional) Reduce the files** – you can subset the fonts with tools like **pyftsubset** if you want a smaller APK, but it is not required for correctness. --- ## 3. Build the style JSON Below is a **minimal style** that demonstrates all the required fields. You can start from any existing style (e.g. the OpenMapTiles demo) and just add the two sections highlighted in **bold**. ```json { "$schema": "https://maplibre.org/maplibre-gl-js/docs/style-spec/", "version": 8, "name": "Offline demo – local fonts only", "sources": { "osm": { "type": "vector", "url": "mbtiles://osm.mbtiles" // <-- your offline vector source } }, /*** 1️⃣ FONT-FACES – map each logical font name to a local file ***/ "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Regular": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0000-00FF", "U+0100-024F"] // Latin, Greek, Cyrillic etc. } ], "Noto Sans Arabic": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0600-06FF", "U+0750-077F", "U+08A0-08FF"] } ], "Noto Sans Devanagari": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] } ], "Noto Sans CJK SC": [ { "url": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf", "unicode-range": ["U+4E00-9FFF", "U+3400-4DBF"] } ] }, /*** 2️⃣ DUMMY GLYPHS URL – required by the spec but never used ***/ "glyphs": "file:///android_asset/empty-glyphs/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "layers": [ { "id": "water", "type": "fill", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "water", "paint": { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" } }, { "id": "place-labels", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], /*** 3️⃣ TEXT-FONT cascade – must match keys in font-faces ***/ "text-font": [ "Noto Sans CJK SC", // CJK first (if any) "Noto Sans Arabic", // Arabic/Hebrew next "Noto Sans Devanagari", // Indic scripts next "Noto Sans Regular" // Latin fallback ], "text-size": 12, "text-anchor": "center" }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ] } ``` ### Why each part matters | Section | What happens at runtime | |---------|--------------------------| | **`glyphs`** | Native will try to fetch `…/Noto%20Sans%20Regular/0-255.pbf` etc. The request will 404 (the `empty-glyphs` folder can be completely empty). The failure is **not fatal** – Native then looks at `font-faces` for the same `text-font` name and loads the local TTF/OTF. | | **`font-faces`** | The `url` is a **file-scheme** that Android’s `AssetManager` can resolve. The `unicode-range` tells HarfBuzz which characters belong to that file; any codepoint outside all ranges will fall back to the (missing) glyph PBFs, which simply means “no glyph → invisible”. Keep the ranges tight to avoid accidental fall-through. | | **`text-font`** | The order is the **fallback cascade**. For a Chinese label the first entry (`Noto Sans CJK SC`) matches the Unicode range, so the CJK font is used. For an Arabic label the second entry matches, etc. If none match, the last entry (`Noto Sans Regular`) is used for Latin text. | --- ## 4. Android-side wiring ### 4.1 Add the MapLibre dependency (≥ 11.13.0) ```gradle implementation 'org.maplibre.gl:android-sdk:11.13.0' // or newer ``` ### 4.2 Load the style from assets (or from a file you downloaded) ```java // 1️⃣ Load the style JSON as a string (assets/style/offline.json) String styleJson = new String( getAssets().open("style/offline.json").readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8); // 2️⃣ Create the map view MapView mapView = findViewById(R.id.mapView); mapView.getMapAsync(map -> { // 3️⃣ Apply the style map.setStyle(new Style.Builder().fromJson(styleJson)); // 4️⃣ (Optional) CJK local-ideograph handling // Native respects the same option as GL-JS: map.setLocalIdeographFontFamily("Noto Sans CJK SC, sans-serif"); }); ``` > **Why we call `setLocalIdeographFontFamily`?** > For CJK, Native will *first* try the `localIdeographFontFamily` (default is the system sans-serif). By setting it to the exact name you used in `font-faces`, you guarantee that the on-device CJK font you bundled is used, not the generic system font. If you omit this call, the system default will be used – still offline, but the visual appearance may differ across devices. ### 4.3 Permissions & CORS * No network permission is needed because everything is local. * The `file://` URLs used in `font-faces` bypass CORS – they are read directly from the app’s assets. If you later serve fonts from a local HTTP server (e.g. `http://127.0.0.1:8080/fonts/...`), you must add the appropriate `android:usesCleartextTraffic="true"` flag or use HTTPS. --- ## 5. Handling special scripts | Script | What you must do in the style | |--------|------------------------------| | **CJK (Chinese, Japanese, Korean)** | *Option A (recommended)* – keep `localIdeographFontFamily` pointing at your bundled CJK font (as shown above). No glyph PBFs needed.
*Option B* – if you really want to use served glyphs (e.g. to match a specific design), set `localIdeographFontFamily: false` in the map options; then the `font-faces` mapping will still be consulted, but you’ll also need a full set of CJK glyph PBFs (huge, not advised for offline). | | **Arabic / Hebrew (RTL)** | No extra plugin is required in Native ≥ 11.13.0. The HarfBuzz engine automatically shapes RTL text when the `text-font` name resolves to a font that contains those glyphs (e.g. `Noto Sans Arabic`). | | **Devanagari, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar, etc.** | These scripts need **grapheme-cluster shaping**. Native does this automatically via HarfBuzz **as long as the font is supplied through `font-faces`**. Do **not** rely on glyph PBFs for these scripts – they will be ignored. | | **Mixed-script labels** (e.g. “北京 Beijing”) | The cascade in `text-font` decides which font is used for each codepoint. Because each script has its own `unicode-range` entry, the correct font will be chosen per character. The fallback order should list the most-specific script first, then the generic Latin fallback. | --- ## 6. Testing & troubleshooting

Description: implicit — Devanagari labels drawn letter by letter
prompt: Hindi labels on my MapLibre GL JS map come out wrong: vowel signs and conjuncts land in the wrong place, as if each letter were drawn on its own. My style has a glyphs URL that serves Noto Sans Devanagari. How do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### TL;DR **Upgrade to a recent MapLibre GL JS version (≥ 6.15.0) and tell the style which Devanagari TTF/OTF to use via the `font-faces` property.** When the style has a `glyphs` URL the Devanagari glyph PBFs are **ignored** – the engine now draws those scripts with the browser’s text-shaping engine. If the browser can’t find a matching font, it falls back to a generic one and you see the “each letter on its own” artefact you described. Below is a step-by-step recipe that fixes the problem for **any MapLibre GL JS map** (also works for MapLibre Native, but the GL JS steps are the ones you need). --- ## 1. Make sure you are on a version that supports proper shaping | Version | What changed for Devanagari (and other complex scripts) | |---------|----------------------------------------------------------| | **< 6.7.0** | Glyph PBFs were used; the engine could only draw one code-point at a time → broken conjuncts. | | **6.7.0 – 6.14.x** | The engine started drawing *grapheme clusters* with the browser, but the fallback was still flaky and many older tutorials still forced the glyph server. | | **≥ 6.15.0** | **All** Devanagari (and other shaping-required scripts) are always rendered by the browser, **even when a `glyphs` URL is present**. The glyph PBFs are simply ignored. | **Action:** ```bash npm i maplibre-gl@^6.15.0 # or use a CDN that points at 6.15.0+ ``` If you are using a CDN, change the script tag to the newest version, e.g.: ```html ``` > **Why this matters:** The “letter-by-letter” artefact you see is exactly the behaviour of the old glyph-PBF path. Upgrading removes that path for Devanagari. --- ## 2. Add a `font-faces` entry that points at a Devanagari TTF/OTF The style must tell MapLibre **which font file** should be used for the `text-font` name you are using (e.g. `"Noto Sans Devanagari Regular"`). The `font-faces` property is read by both GL JS and Native and works the same way browsers resolve `@font-face`. ### 2.1. Choose a font file * **Recommended:** Google’s *Noto Sans Devanagari* (free, covers the whole block). Download the TTF from the Noto repo: `https://github.com/googlefonts/noto-fonts/blob/main/hinted/ttf/NotoSansDevanagari/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf` * **Alternative:** Any other Devanagari OTF/TTF you prefer (e.g. *Mukta Vaani*, *Lohit Devanagari*). ### 2.2. Host the file where the browser can fetch it If you already have a static-asset server (e.g. the same origin that serves your style JSON), copy the file there: ``` /fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf ``` Make sure CORS headers allow `GET` from your map page (most CDNs do this automatically). ### 2.3. Declare it in the style Add (or extend) the top-level `font-faces` object in your style JSON: ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": "https://example.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", // you can keep this; it will be ignored for Devanagari "font-faces": { "Noto Sans Devanagari Regular": [ { "url": "https://example.com/fonts/NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf", "unicode-range": ["U+0900-097F"] // Devanagari block } ] }, "layers": [ { "id": "place-labels-hi", "type": "symbol", "source": "osm", "source-layer": "place", "filter": ["==", "$type", "Point"], "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name:hi"], // Hindi name property "text-font": ["Noto Sans Devanagari Regular"], // must match the key above "text-size": 12, "text-anchor": "center" }, "paint": { "text-color": "#222" } } ] } ``` **Key points** * The **key** in `font-faces` (`"Noto Sans Devanagari Regular"`) **must be exactly the same string** you use in `text-font`. * The `unicode-range` limits the file to Devanagari code points; you can omit it, but keeping it makes the style clearer and helps the engine skip the file for other scripts. * You can still keep the `glyphs` URL for Latin, Arabic, etc.; it will be used only for scripts that *do* rely on SDF glyphs. --- ## 3. (Optional) Remove the `glyphs` URL for a pure-local-fonts style If you never need SDF glyphs (i.e. you are happy with the browser’s rendering for all scripts), you can **omit** the `glyphs` field entirely. GL JS ≥ 5.11.0 treats this as “local-fonts-only mode” and will never try to fetch PBFs. ```json { "version": 8, // "glyphs": "...", <-- delete this line "font-faces": { … } } ``` *Pros:* No network requests for glyphs, works offline, no CORS headaches. *Cons:* You lose the ability to use SDF-scaled glyphs for scripts that *do* need them (e.g. Latin on very high-DPI screens). Keep the field if you still want SDF for those. --- ## 4. Verify the result 1. **Open the map** in a modern browser (Chrome ≥ 108, Firefox ≥ 106, Safari ≥ 15). 2. Inspect a Hindi label with a vowel sign or a conjunct (e.g. “क्ष”). 3. The glyph should be a single, correctly-shaped unit, not a stack of separate letters. If you still see the broken layout: | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | **No Devanagari characters at all (blank)** | Font file not reachable or CORS blocked | Open the font URL directly in the browser → should download. Add `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain) on the server. | | **Wrong font (looks like a generic sans-serif)** | `text-font` name does not match the `font-faces` key | Double-check spelling, case, and spaces. | | **Still letter-by-letter** | Still using an old GL JS version (< 6.15) | Verify the script tag / npm version. | | **Mixed fonts (some letters from one font, others from another)** | Multiple `text-font` entries where the first matches a local font and the second falls back to glyphs | Keep only the Devanagari entry for Hindi layers, or ensure the first entry is the Devanagari font you declared. | --- ## 5. What about the `glyphs` server you already have? You *can* keep the existing Noto Sans Devanagari PBFs on your glyph server; they will simply be ignored for Devanagari text. This is harmless, but you may want to: * **Remove them** to save storage/bandwidth, **or** * **Leave them** if you also serve other scripts (Latin, Arabic) from the same server and want to keep a single endpoint. --- ## 6. Full minimal example (CDN + local font) ```html Hindi labels – correct shaping
``` *The map will now render Hindi place names with proper vowel signs, ligatures, and conjuncts.* --- ## 7. Quick checklist (copy-paste into your notes) - [ ] **Upgrade** to `maplibre-gl@>=6.15.0`. - [ ] **Host** a Devanagari TTF/OTF (e.g. NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf). - [ ] Add a **`font-faces`** entry that maps the exact `text-font` name you use to that URL, with a `unicode-range` covering `U+0900-097F`. - [ ] Ensure **CORS** allows the browser to fetch the font file. - [ ] In your layer, set `"text-font": ["Noto Sans Devanagari Regular"]`. - [ ] (Optional) **Remove** the `glyphs` field if you want a pure-local-fonts style. - [ ] Test; if letters still look broken, double-check version and spelling. --- ### TL;DR again 1. **Use MapLibre GL JS ≥ 6.15.0** (new shaping engine). 2. **Declare the Devanagari TTF via `font-faces`** and reference it in `text-font`. 3. **Leave the `glyphs` URL** (it will be ignored) **or drop it** for a fully local-fonts style. After those two changes Hindi labels will be rendered correctly, with vowel signs and conjuncts positioned exactly as they appear in native text editors. Happy mapping!

Description: negative — out-of-scope question about hillshade/terrain layers
prompt: How do I add a hillshade layer from a raster-dem source to my MapLibre GL JS style?
